source.title: The combinatorics of discrete time-trees: theory and open problems

accepted.question_text: A discrete time-tree is a rooted binary phylogenetic tree on a fixed labeled leaf set in which every node is assigned a distinct non-negative integer time and each child has smaller time than its parent. The paper studies graph families on such trees, including DtTm, DtTum, RNNI, and RNNIu, where two trees are adjacent when one can be obtained from the other by one allowed local move such as changing the length of one event interval by 1, swapping the ranks of two nodes that bound a unit-length interval, or performing a nearest-neighbor interchange move on a unit-length interval, with graph-specific restrictions. Given two discrete time-trees in one of these graph families, what is the computational complexity of computing their graph distance, meaning the minimum number of allowed moves needed to transform one tree into the other?
accepted.context_brief: Distance complexity in discrete time-tree graphs

evidence.quote: A discrete time-tree is a tree such that all its nodes are assigned distinct times from the set of non-negative integers and every node has a smaller time than its parent

Two trees T and R are adjacent in DtTm if R can be obtained from T by one of three operations: a length move performed on interval I, swapping the rank of two nodes x and y on interval I or an NNI move performed on interval I
Problem 1 What is the complexity of computing the distance between two discrete time-trees?

accepted.question_text: Consider any of the discrete time-tree graph families DtT, DtTu, RNNI, or RNNIu on a fixed leaf set. Suppose two trees T and R share a split, meaning that each tree has an edge whose removal induces the same bipartition of the leaves. Must every shortest path from T to R in the chosen graph stay entirely within trees that continue to display that shared split?
accepted.context_brief: Split theorem for ranked and timed tree graphs

evidence.quote: Hence, a natural question that would contribute to understanding Problem 1 is whether or not the Split Theorem holds in the RNNI graph and other time-tree graphs.

The latter claims were mainly based on the so-called Split Theorem which states the following: If a partition of leaves given by an edge is shared between two trees then there exists a shortest NNI path between the trees such that every tree on the path maintains the partition.

Conjecture 9 The following is true in all graphs DtT, DtTu, RNNI, and RNNIu, but not in NNI. If a partition of leaves given by an edge is presented in two trees T and R then the partition is presented in every tree on every shortest path between T and R.
